Lessons.Title: Analyze Subtraction Algorithms
ExplanationParagraphs: Analyze subtraction algorithms by deciding when to decompose (exchange) place-value units. The original 2021 lesson compares an algorithm that decomposes first with one that subtracts from the ones column and only decomposes when necessary. Use mathematical reasoning, not a mechanically memorized shortcut.

Warm-up — Number Talk, 10 minutes: calculate 400−200=200, 450−200=250, 450−205=245, and 450−215=235 mentally. Tell the teacher how subtracting an additional 5 or 10 ones alters an otherwise similar difference.

Activity 1 — Compare Two Subtraction Algorithms, 20 minutes. The source shows the first step for two methods before asking partners to apply both to 824−541=283. Algorithm A starts by checking which place-value columns need decomposition and performs exchanges before subtraction. Algorithm B proceeds right-to-left, exchanging only when a column cannot be subtracted directly.

For 824−541, calculate 4−1=3 ones, and 2 tens cannot remove 4 tens. Trade one of 8 hundreds for ten tens so 8 hundreds,2 tens become 7 hundreds,12 tens. Now 12−4=8 tens and 7−5=2 hundreds. Thus 824−541=283. In algorithm A the exchange is established before taking any differences; in algorithm B the exchange happens on reaching the tens column.

The partner discussion asks whether one strategy is easier to keep organized. Method A permits the teacher to check all necessary exchanges first and may work from either side; Method B allows subtraction to start immediately and trades units only if needed. Both must conserve value. Discuss original two algorithm illustrations with the teacher; these are independently worded explanations, not copies of source images.

Activity 2 — Use an Algorithm?, 15 minutes: Noah attempts 301−167. Elena says 0 tens means there are not enough ones to subtract 7. Think about this statement: exchange a hundred for 10 tens, then exchange one ten for 10 ones. Rewrite 301 as 2 hundreds, 9 tens and 11 ones.

After regrouping, subtract 11−7=4 ones, 9−6=3 tens, 2−1=1 hundred, so 301−167=134. Present this in expanded blocks and in one written algorithm. Revisit Elena's claim: the algorithm works when the decompositions are correctly recorded, even though the original tens digit was zero.

Use MLR8 Discussion Supports to restate a partner's thinking and use correct phrases 'one hundred equals ten tens' and 'one ten equals ten ones.' A correct scalar does not prove the original teacher-led comparison and explanation were completed.

Synthesis: contrast pre-decomposition with on-demand decomposition, then identify an advantage of each, without declaring a single method compulsory. Original publisher images remain with publisher; original gated Subtraction Reflection Cool-down is not reproduced. Edulytics separately assesses 301−167=134 and checks reasoning with a teacher.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exchange before subtracting
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inspect all necessary tens/hundreds exchanges first.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Exchange one hundred for ten tens or a ten for ten ones before calculating differences.
KeyConcepts.Example: 824−541: decompose 8 hundreds and 2 tens into 7 hundreds and 12 tens, then subtract 283.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exchange when necessary
KeyConcepts.Definition: Start subtracting in the ones column; only exchange when a lower place does not have enough units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The total value must remain invariant at every step.

KeyConcepts.Title: Algorithm comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two different step orders can implement the same equivalent place-value mathematics.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A valid method conserves the original minuend's value and matches the context.

WorkedExamples.Title: Algorithm A and B on the same subtraction
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 824−541 with both orderings of decomposition.
Steps: The tens cannot subtract 4 tens from 2 tens. Exchange a hundred into ten tens.
Now subtract 4−1=3 ones, 12−4=8 tens, and 7−5=2 hundreds.

WorkedExamples.Title: Exchanging across a zero
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 301−167 and explain Elena's zero-tens concern.
WorkedExamples.Method: Exchange a hundred into tens and one of those tens into ones.
Steps: 3 hundreds 0 tens 1 one become 2 hundreds 10 tens 1 one.
Exchange one ten: 2 hundreds, 9 tens and 11 ones.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original mental subtraction warm-up
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 450−215 using the previous warm-up expression 450−205.
WorkedExamples.Method: Subtract ten more from a known difference
WorkedExamples.Check: 215+235=450; a teacher still checks student reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtracting 7 ones from 1 without decomposing in 301−167.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One one is insufficient, and there are initially zero tens.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Trade a hundred for ten tens, then trade a ten for ten ones, giving 11 ones.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Trading a hundred into ten tens without decreasing the hundreds count.
Treating the two source algorithms as different arithmetic rules.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Both exchange ten units for one larger unit of equal value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare when exchanges are recorded, not the numerical result.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-certifying class discussion after checking 134 or 283.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original explanation about sequence and tradeoffs is teacher-led.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the separate process rubric for algorithm steps and partner explanation.

SummaryPoints: Method A decomposes first; Method B decomposes when the column needs additional units.
Across zero: 301−167=134 by exchanging a hundred and a ten.
The independent Edulytics Cool-down assesses 301−167=134; the publisher's gated original prompt was not read.
